MOTS-c: The Mitochondria-Derived Exercise Peptide — Research Dossier

Research compounds discussed for educational purposes. Not FDA-approved for human use. No completed Phase 2 efficacy trial in humans exists as of November 2026. Consult a healthcare provider before use.

What Is MOTS-c?

MOTS-c — short for Mitochondrial Open Reading Frame of the 12S rRNA-c — is a 16-amino acid peptide discovered in 2015 by Dr. Pinchas Cohen and colleagues at the USC Leonard Davis School of Gerontology. What makes MOTS-c extraordinary is its origin: its coding sequence is not found in the nuclear genome but inside the mitochondrial genome — specifically within the small ribosomal RNA gene (12S rRNA) of human mitochondrial DNA. This makes MOTS-c a founding member of a newly identified class of signaling molecules called mitochondria-derived peptides (MDPs).

For decades, the mitochondrial genome was thought to encode only the core subunits of respiratory chain complexes and two ribosomal RNAs — nothing more. The Cohen lab's 2015 discovery (Cell Metabolism) revealed that a small open reading frame inside the 12S rRNA gene encodes a secreted peptide hormone that the body uses to signal metabolic stress and regulate whole-body metabolism. The fact that MOTS-c's sequence has been conserved across species from C. elegans to humans suggests strong evolutionary pressure — the mitochondria have been broadcasting this metabolic alarm signal for hundreds of millions of years.

Circulating MOTS-c levels in humans rise with acute exercise and decline with aging and type 2 diabetes. This natural pattern has positioned it as a central focus of research into exercise-mimetic pharmacology and longevity biology.

Mechanism of Action

MOTS-c activates AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) — the master metabolic energy sensor — via a pathway distinct from the canonical AMP/ATP ratio mechanism that governs most AMPK activation:

  • AICAR-independent AMPK activation: In skeletal muscle, MOTS-c stimulates AMPK without changing AMP:ATP ratios, suggesting it operates through a parallel signaling branch that remains active even when canonical AMPK signals are suppressed.
  • Nuclear translocation under stress: Under metabolic stress (high fat diet, glucose deprivation, aging), MOTS-c translocates from the cytoplasm to the nucleus, where it directly activates the antioxidant response element (ARE) pathway via Nrf2 transcription factor. This nuclear activity triggers a broad anti-oxidant and metabolic gene expression program.
  • Glucose uptake enhancement: MOTS-c stimulates GLUT4 translocation to the cell surface in skeletal muscle, increasing insulin-independent glucose uptake — the same end goal as exercise-mediated AMPK activation.
  • Fatty acid oxidation: AMPK activation by MOTS-c suppresses fatty acid synthesis and promotes beta-oxidation, reducing lipid accumulation in metabolically active tissues.

The net result is an integrated metabolic improvement: improved insulin sensitivity, increased glucose disposal, reduced adiposity, and reduced oxidative stress — a profile that partially recapitulates the metabolic signature of regular aerobic exercise.

Key Research Findings

Foundational Discovery (Lee et al., Cell Metabolism, 2015)

MOTS-c was administered to mice on a high-fat diet. Results: significantly improved insulin tolerance, reduced fasting glucose, reduced adipose tissue accumulation, and improved euglycemic hyperinsulinemic clamp parameters vs. saline-treated controls. This established MOTS-c as a metabolically active peptide in a mammalian model.

Exercise Mimetic Properties (Kim et al., Cell Metabolism, 2018)

Aging mice (12 months) given MOTS-c injections showed improved running capacity and grip strength comparable to voluntary exercise training cohorts, without formal exercise. MOTS-c restored age-related decline in muscle mitochondrial function and shifted skeletal muscle metabolism toward fatty acid oxidation. This paper introduced the concept of MOTS-c as a pharmacological exercise mimetic.

Lifespan Extension in Aged Mice (Nature Communications)

MOTS-c administered to 23-month-old male mice (a late-life intervention after the equivalent of human age ~65) extended median lifespan by approximately 11%. This late-life benefit implies that MOTS-c supplementation may have utility even when initiated after the natural age-related decline in endogenous levels has begun.

Human Observational Evidence (Reynolds et al., Nature Communications, 2021)

The most robust human data comes from Reynolds et al., who measured MOTS-c in skeletal muscle biopsies and blood samples from 10 healthy young men before and after acute cycling exercise. Key findings:

  • Skeletal muscle MOTS-c levels rose approximately 12-fold after acute exercise
  • Plasma MOTS-c rose approximately 1.6-fold after exercise
  • Cross-sectional data confirmed lower MOTS-c levels in older adults vs. young adults
  • T2D patients had lower MOTS-c levels vs. age-matched healthy controls

These observations firmly establish MOTS-c as a human exercise-responsive, age-declining metabolic peptide — but do not constitute evidence that injecting exogenous MOTS-c into humans reproduces the metabolic benefits seen in mice.

Regulatory Milestone (2026)

The FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) voted 7-2 on July 24, 2026 to recommend MOTS-c for placement on the 503A Bulks List, which would permit licensed compounding pharmacies to prepare MOTS-c for patients. Following this advisory vote, HHS issued an Interim Enforcement Discretion Policy (approximately October 28, 2026) directing FDA not to take enforcement action against state-licensed compounding pharmacies preparing MOTS-c (and five other peptides: BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, Epitalon, Semax) under specific quality and labeling conditions. This policy shift is the direct regulatory trigger for this dossier entry.

Dosing in Research

In mouse studies, MOTS-c has been administered at doses of 5–15 mg/kg body weight by intraperitoneal or subcutaneous injection, typically daily or every other day. Translating these doses to humans is imprecise: standard interspecies scaling (Km factor) suggests rough human-equivalent doses in the range of 0.5–1.5 mg/kg, though no Phase 2 dose-finding data in humans is available to validate this.

The MOTS-MET Phase 2a trial (NCT07505745, recruiting) is testing a specific dose in humans for 12 weeks — the trial design has not been published as of November 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is MOTS-c and why is it called a mitochondria-derived peptide?

MOTS-c is a 16-amino acid peptide whose coding sequence is located inside the mitochondrial genome — specifically within the 12S ribosomal RNA gene of human mitochondrial DNA. This makes it a member of a newly discovered class of signaling molecules called mitochondria-derived peptides (MDPs). For most of the 20th century, it was thought the mitochondrial genome only encoded respiratory chain complex subunits. The 2015 discovery by USC's Pinchas Cohen lab revealed a small open reading frame inside the 12S rRNA gene encodes a secreted signaling peptide that communicates the mitochondria's metabolic state to the rest of the cell and to systemic circulation. MOTS-c is now one of several identified MDPs (including humanin and SHLPs 1-6), each with distinct functions — but MOTS-c is the most studied in exercise, metabolism, and lifespan.

What did the FDA advisory committee vote in July 2026 mean for MOTS-c access?

The FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) voted 7-2 on July 24, 2026 to recommend placing MOTS-c on the 503A Bulks List. If finalized, this would permit FDA-registered compounding pharmacies to legally prepare MOTS-c for patient use even though no commercial FDA-approved product exists. Following the advisory vote, HHS issued an Interim Enforcement Discretion Policy (~October 28, 2026) directing FDA not to take enforcement action against state-licensed pharmacies compounding MOTS-c under specific quality and labeling conditions. This is a significant regulatory shift: prior to this policy, compounding pharmacies faced legal uncertainty about MOTS-c. After it, pharmacies can prepare MOTS-c for patient prescriptions with reduced regulatory risk. It does NOT mean MOTS-c is FDA-approved — it has no approved indication, no approved product, and no completed Phase 2 efficacy trial.

What is the strongest human evidence for MOTS-c's metabolic effects?

The strongest direct human evidence is observational. Reynolds et al. (Nature Communications, 2021) measured MOTS-c levels in skeletal muscle biopsies and blood from 10 healthy young men before and after acute exercise. MOTS-c rose approximately 12-fold in skeletal muscle and 1.6-fold in circulation after exercise — confirming the human body increases MOTS-c production in response to physical activity. Cross-sectional studies show plasma MOTS-c is significantly lower in older adults and T2D patients vs. younger or metabolically healthy controls. These data establish MOTS-c as an exercise-responsive, age-declining signal in humans. What they do NOT establish is that injecting exogenous MOTS-c into humans reproduces benefits seen in mice. No completed randomized controlled trial of exogenous MOTS-c supplementation in humans has been published as of November 2026. The MOTS-MET Phase 2a trial (120 adults with prediabetes, 12-week) is designed to answer this question.

Research Limitations

  • No completed human efficacy trials: All beneficial metabolic effects have been demonstrated in rodent models. The critical question — whether injected MOTS-c reproduces these effects in humans — awaits the MOTS-MET Phase 2a trial (results expected 2027).
  • Small human observational studies: The key human evidence (Reynolds et al.) involved 10 subjects. Cross-sectional MOTS-c level associations are correlational, not causal.
  • FDA staff opposition: FDA scientific staff recommended against MOTS-c's inclusion on the 503A Bulks List due to lack of human clinical studies. The 7-2 favorable vote by the advisory committee was an advisory (non-binding) recommendation; the full regulatory pathway to formal 503A listing is pending.
  • Unknown human dosing: No Phase 2 dose-finding data in humans exists. Mouse-to-human dose translation for MOTS-c has not been validated.
  • Measurement challenges: Commercial MOTS-c assays vary in specificity; plasma levels are low and may be confounded by cross-reactivity. The reliability of circulating MOTS-c as a biomarker requires further validation.
